section.title: The Cost, the Storm, and the Demoniacs
section.sectionRationale: The miracle collection continues, now showing the King's authority over the deepest powers and the cost of following Him. Two would-be followers meet the hard demands of discipleship; a violent storm is stilled by His word; and two demoniacs are freed across the lake. In each scene the question rises: what kind of man is this, before whom sea and demons yield?
section.thesis: Jesus, the homeless Son of Man whose claim outweighs every other loyalty, wields the authority of God over wind, wave, and demonic powers, so that following Him is both supremely costly and utterly safe, since the One who calls is Lord of creation and the spirit world.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the cost of following the Son of Man; the stilling of the storm and the disciples' wonder; and the deliverance of the two demoniacs and the town's rejection.

units.label: The cost of following
units.note: the Son of Man has no place to lay His head

verses.text: When Jesus saw a large crowd around Him, He gave orders to cross to the other side of the sea.
And one of the scribes came to Him and said, “Teacher, I will {{akoloutheo|follow}} You wherever You go.”
Jesus replied, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the {{huiosanthropou|Son of Man}} has no place to lay His head.”
Another of His disciples requested, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.”
But Jesus told him, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”

units.label: The storm stilled
units.note: even the winds and the sea obey Him

verses.text: When He got into the boat, His disciples followed Him.
Suddenly a violent storm came up on the sea, so that the boat was engulfed by the waves. But Jesus was sleeping.
The disciples went and woke Him, saying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!”
“You of little faith,” Jesus replied, “why are you so afraid?” Then He got up and {{epitimao|rebuked}} the winds and the sea, and it was perfectly calm.
The men were amazed and asked, “What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!”

units.label: The demoniacs freed
units.note: Son of God, before the appointed time

verses.text: When Jesus arrived on the other side in the region of the Gadarenes, He was met by two demon-possessed men coming from the tombs. They were so violent that no one could pass that way.
“What do You want with us, {{huiostheou|Son of God}}?” they shouted. “Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?”
In the distance a large herd of pigs was feeding.
So the demons begged Jesus, “If You drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.”
“Go!” He told them. So they came out and went into the pigs, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the waters.
Those tending the pigs ran off into the town and reported all this, including the account of the demon-possessed men.
Then the whole town went out to meet Jesus. And when they saw Him, they begged Him to leave their region.

akoloutheo.gloss: To follow, come after as a disciple. The scribe volunteers to follow anywhere; Jesus tests the eagerness by naming the homelessness it involves. To follow Him is to attach one's whole life to a Master who had nowhere to lay His head.

huiosanthropou.gloss: The Son of Man, Jesus' favored self-title, drawn from Daniel 7 where one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion. It holds together His true humanity, His present lowliness, and His coming glory and judgment.

epitimao.gloss: To rebuke, command with authority. Jesus rebukes the winds and sea as He rebukes demons, treating the raging chaos as something under His command. In the Old Testament it is the LORD who rebukes and stills the sea, Psalm 106:9.

huiostheou.gloss: Son of God. Ironically, the demons confess Jesus' divine identity that the townspeople miss. They know who He is and that He is their judge, dreading torment before the appointed day of final judgment.

basic.context: Jesus prepares to cross the Sea of Galilee. Two men speak of following Him, and He confronts them with the cost: the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head, and following Him must come before every other tie. In the boat a violent storm nearly swamps them while Jesus sleeps; He wakes, rebukes the wind and sea, and stuns the disciples. Across the lake He frees two violent demoniacs, but the frightened town begs Him to leave.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the three scenes together: each answers the question what kind of man is this. The demands of discipleship, the stilling of the storm, and the mastery of demons all reveal a Jesus of divine authority whose claim on His followers is total. Notice that the disciples' fear is rebuked as little faith, and the demons confess what humans miss.
basic.originalLanguages: To follow Jesus is to attach one's whole life to Him, even into homelessness. He calls Himself the Son of Man, Daniel's figure of lowliness now and dominion to come. He rebukes the winds and sea with the same word He uses on demons, the authority the Old Testament ascribes to the LORD. And the demons, terrified, confess Him Son of God and their judge.
basic.typology: Jesus stilling the sea takes up what only God does in the Old Testament, mastering the chaos waters, so the disciples' question, what kind of man is this, has a staggering answer. The Son of Man recalls Daniel 7, the one given everlasting dominion. And His authority over demons signals that the kingdom of God is overthrowing the kingdom of darkness.
basic.christ: Jesus is revealed as the divine Lord: the One whose word the wind and waves obey, whom the demons dread as their appointed judge, and whose call outranks every human loyalty. He is the lowly Son of Man now, homeless and asleep in a boat, yet the sovereign King who will come in glory. To follow Him is costly, but He is completely trustworthy.
basic.god: The God who rebukes the sea and rules the deep is present in Jesus. He is Lord over the forces that terrify us, chaos, death, and the demonic, and none of them can act apart from His permission. He calls His people to a discipleship that puts Him first, and He is worthy of it, being the Lord of creation and the spirit world.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 107 pictures the LORD stilling the storm for terrified sailors. Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man who receives dominion. Job 38 shows God commanding the sea's boundaries. And James 2 says even the demons believe and shudder, as they do here.
basic.oneStory: The King moves through His world revealing who He is. He calls followers to a total, costly allegiance, then shows why He is worth it: the wind and sea obey Him, and the powers of darkness tremble and flee at His word. The lowly Son of Man asleep in the boat is the Lord who rules chaos and hell, and the whole scene presses the reader toward the disciples' awestruck question and its answer: this is the Son of God.

context.literary:
Matthew has arranged these verses with a clear hand. The boat is the frame: 'He gave orders to cross to the other side,' verse 18, begins the journey, and Jesus' arrival 'on the other side,' verse 28, ends it. Inside the frame the three scenes are bound by two words that echo. The first is follow. The scribe says, 'I will follow You,' verse 19, Jesus says to the second man, 'Follow Me,' verse 22, and then, when Jesus gets into the boat, 'His disciples followed Him,' verse 23. The man who talked of following stays on the shore, and those who actually follow find themselves in a storm. The second is the question about identity. The disciples ask, 'What kind of man is this?' verse 27, and in the very next scene the demons answer, 'Son of God,' verse 29. The reader hears from the voice of hell what the boat could not say.

The storm is told in a compressed pattern that Matthew uses elsewhere: danger, cry, rebuke, and calm, with the little rebuke to the disciples placed before the rebuke of the sea, verse 26, unlike the other Gospels, which reverse the order. A great shaking in verse 24 meets a great calm in verse 26, the same adjective on both sides, so that the size of the threat is matched by the size of the peace.

The demoniacs scene is a tale of contrasts: men who are uncontrollable, a Lord who needs only one word, 'Go!', and a town that is more afraid of the cure than of the disease. Matthew's account is much shorter than Mark's or Luke's. It leaves out the name Legion and the man's later mission, Mark 5:9 and 19, and stays on the two main questions of power and response. Together, the three scenes are a short course in who Jesus is and what following Him costs.
context.historical:
The Sea of Galilee lies about two hundred metres below sea level, ringed by hills, and cold air funnelling down through the ravines can whip up violent squalls with little warning. Several of the disciples were professional fishermen who knew the lake well, which gives their terror its weight. A fishing boat of the first century was a small open vessel, and 'engulfed' is the right word for what the waves did to it.

The scribe was a teacher of the law, and his offer to follow is unusual, for disciples normally chose a rabbi, not the reverse, and a scribe would be giving up status to follow a wandering preacher. The reply about foxes and birds tells him what that status will cost him. The second man's request to bury his father touches one of the weightiest duties of Jewish life. Burial was a sacred obligation, taking precedence over many other duties; Joseph asked leave to bury Jacob, Genesis 50:5, and the law allowed a priest to defile himself for the nearest relatives, Leviticus 21:1 to 3, though a Nazirite could not, Numbers 6:6 and 7. Jesus' answer therefore lays His claim above the most honoured of family duties.

The region of the Gadarenes lay on the east side of the lake, in a largely Gentile area. The BSB footnote notes that other manuscripts read Gerasenes or Gergesenes, which is why the Gospels give different names for what must be the same district, the territory attached to a nearby city. Pigs were unclean for Jews, Leviticus 11:7, and a herd of them says that the area was Gentile. Tombs were places of death and impurity, and Isaiah 65:4 describes rebellious people 'sitting among the graves' and 'eating the meat of pigs,' a grim setting for the men's lives. Mark and Luke tell of a single man; Matthew tells of two, and the two accounts do not contradict each other, since mentioning one does not deny the other.
context.canonical:
The stilling of the storm belongs to the oldest strand of Israel's worship. The LORD 'rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up,' Psalm 106:9, and 'rebukes the sea and dries it up,' Nahum 1:4. 'You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them,' Psalm 89:9, and 'You stilled the roaring of the seas,' Psalm 65:7. Psalm 107:23 to 30, in which sailors in a tempest cry out and He 'calmed the storm to a whisper,' is the closest pattern, and Job 38:8 to 11 has the LORD setting the sea's boundaries. In Scripture the sea can stand for chaos, and God's mastery of it is a sign of who He is, Job 26:12 and Isaiah 51:9 and 10. When Jesus does what the psalms say only God does, the disciples' question is the right one.

The Son of Man title is Daniel's, 'One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven,' who received 'an everlasting dominion,' Daniel 7:13 and 14. Matthew 8:20 is the first time in this Gospel that Jesus uses it, and He uses it of homelessness, a double portrait of humiliation and glory that will run through the book, Matthew 24:30.

The demons' cry that Jesus has come 'before the appointed time' belongs to the New Testament's view that their judgment is set, Matthew 25:41, 2 Peter 2:4 and Revelation 20:10. Luke shows them begging not to be sent into the Abyss, Luke 8:31. Jesus' words in Matthew 12:28 and 29, that the kingdom has come when He drives out demons and that He has tied up the strong man, are the explanation of what happens in the territory of the Gadarenes.

Finally, the same boat appears again in Matthew 14:22 to 33, where Peter's cry 'Lord, if it is You' leads to the confession, 'Truly You are the Son of God,' Matthew 14:33. The scene on the sea in Matthew 8 is the first step of that road.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew's readers were a community of Jesus' followers living under pressure, and he wanted them to hear three things in this short passage.

First, that the road of discipleship is real and costly, and that Jesus does not hide the price. He is not recruiting by flattery. He tells the scribe that to follow Him is to give up security, and He tells the second man that no tie, however sacred, can come first. Matthew leaves both men's response unrecorded. He does not tell us what they did, because he wants his readers to answer the question for themselves.

Second, that the disciples' experience in the storm is the church's experience. The boat is in danger, and the Lord appears to be asleep. Matthew's readers, who were facing storms of their own, are meant to hear 'Lord, save us!' as their own prayer, and the answer as the pattern of their hope: the one who is in the boat is the one who rules the wind. The rebuke 'You of little faith' is a mild one, for the faith that cries out is real, though weak.

Third, that Jesus' authority extends over every power that threatens people, the natural world and the demonic, and that He is in every case the Son of God. This is the climax of the miracle cycle, and Matthew wants his readers to leave the scene with the disciples' question ringing in their ears, so that when they come to the next chapters, they will know the answer.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes one crossing of the lake and one encounter in Gentile territory. The conditions of discipleship in verses 19 to 22 are addressed to two particular men, but Matthew includes them because they apply to everyone, and Jesus repeats them in Matthew 10:37 and 38 and 16:24. They are not a mandate to abandon the care of aged parents, for Jesus Himself condemned the evasion of that duty, Mark 7:9 to 13. They are a statement that nothing may stand ahead of Him.

The storm does not promise that following Jesus will keep believers out of storms. The disciples were in the storm because they were following Him, and that is the point. It also does not say that every storm will be calmed on request. It shows that the Lord is present in the boat and that His presence outweighs the waves.

The destruction of the pigs is a record of what happened, not a pattern for dealing with animals or property, and the town's request that Jesus leave is a description of a response, not a model for one. The man who was healed in Mark's account is told to go home and tell what the Lord has done for him, Mark 5:19, which shows what the right response looks like.

debates.question: What does 'let the dead bury their own dead' mean?

views.label: The spiritually dead can bury the physically dead
views.case: The second 'dead' are people who are dead to the kingdom, and the saying makes the point that following Jesus is a matter of life, and nothing else is as urgent. It uses a deliberate play on words to shock the hearer into seeing the priority.

views.label: A vivid demand that no duty may delay obedience
views.case: The man may not have been about to bury a father who had died; the phrase may mean that he wanted to wait until his father died, perhaps years away. Either way, the point is that nothing may come between the call and the answer, as Luke 9:59 to 62 also shows. Elijah allowed Elisha to say goodbye to his parents, 1 Kings 19:20, but the one who calls here is greater than Elijah.

debates.bearing: Both readings hold that Christ's claim comes before every other claim. They also agree that Jesus does not teach contempt for family, but He will not be second to it.

debates.question: Why did Jesus let the demons enter the pigs, and why did the town react as it did?

views.label: It showed the demons' destructive intent and Jesus' complete authority
views.case: The herd's rush into the sea shows what the demons would have done to the men, and it shows that they could act only by His permission. The two men's freedom was worth far more than the herd, and the sea swallowed what the demons had made unclean.

views.label: It exposed what the townspeople valued
views.case: The town went out to meet Jesus and begged Him to leave, which suggests that the loss of the herd and the presence of a power they could not control were more disturbing than the restoration of two men who had terrorised the road. The scene tests where each heart stands.

debates.bearing: Both views share the point that Jesus values persons over property, and that His presence forces a decision. Some, as in this town, would rather He went away.

debates.question: Is the stilling of the storm mainly about Christ's identity or about faith in life's storms?

views.label: It reveals who Jesus is
views.case: The disciples' question in verse 27 is the point of the story, and the Old Testament background, Psalm 107:29 and Psalm 89:9, makes the answer plain: only the LORD rules the sea. The passage is first about Christology, and only then about discipleship.

views.label: It teaches how disciples should meet fear
views.case: The rebuke 'You of little faith' and the question 'why are you so afraid?' are directed at the disciples' response, and the church has long read the boat as a picture of its own life. Matthew's disciples are following, and in the following they meet the storm.

debates.bearing: The two readings are complementary. The comfort of the second depends on the truth of the first: the storm is safe to face because of who is in the boat.

study.originalLanguages:
The scribe addresses Jesus as didaskale, 'Teacher,' verse 19, while the disciple of verse 21 says kyrie, 'Lord.' In Matthew the title Teacher is often used by those outside the circle of discipleship, as in 9:11, 12:38 and 22:16, while 'Lord' is the address of those who follow. The scribe offers to follow 'wherever You go,' and Jesus answers by naming where He goes: to places with no den or nest. The word for the foxes' dens is a plain word for burrows, and the word for the birds' nests means a place to lodge. Jesus, who is greater than both fox and bird, has no such place.

The storm is called seismos megas, literally 'a great shaking,' verse 24. Matthew uses seismos elsewhere for earthquakes, 24:7, 27:54 and 28:2, so the word suggests that the whole created order is convulsed. The stilling that follows is galene megale, 'a great calm,' verse 26, with the same adjective, so that the shaking and the calm are the same size. The disciples' cry is sozon, 'save,' and apollymetha, 'we are perishing,' two verbs that sound like a prayer more than an alarm.

Jesus calls them oligopistoi, 'little faith,' verse 26. This is a word Matthew loves, using it at 6:30, 8:26, 14:31 and 16:8. It never means no faith. It describes people who do trust but whose trust has not yet reached the weight of the circumstances. The word epitimao, 'rebuked,' is the same word used for the commands to demons and the one in Psalm 106:9 of the Greek Old Testament, where the LORD 'rebuked' the Red Sea.

The demons' cry, 'What do You want with us,' translates a Hebrew idiom that appears in the Old Testament, as in 1 Kings 17:18, and means 'What have we in common?' It is a protest at the intrusion of someone who does not belong to their world. They ask whether He has come to basanisai, 'to torment,' before the proper time, and the phrase pro kairou, 'before the time,' shows that they know a time is set.

A small contrast of verbs ties the end to the middle. The demons parakaloun, 'begged,' Jesus in verse 31 to be sent into the pigs, and the townspeople parekalesan, 'begged,' Him in verse 34 to leave. The same verb is used for two opposite requests, and Jesus grants the first and honours the second. Finally the phrase 'Son of Man' is huios tou anthropou, and 'Son of God' is huios tou theou. The title of humiliation and the title of divinity appear in the same chapter, in the mouths of different speakers, and they describe the same person.

typology.type: The one who stills the sea
typology.fulfillment: In the Old Testament only the LORD stills the waves, Psalm 89:9 and Psalm 107:29, and rules the chaos waters that threaten creation, Job 38:8 to 11. In the boat, Jesus does it with a word. Jonah too slept through a storm, Jonah 1:5, and the captain woke him and told him to call on his God; the storm stopped when he was thrown overboard, Jonah 1:15. Jesus, who is 'greater than Jonah,' Matthew 12:41, wakes up by His own power and stills the storm Himself. The correspondence is of a sleeper in a boat and a calmed sea. The escalation is that Jesus is not the cause of the storm but its master, and does not need to be sacrificed to quiet it. The type falls short in that Jonah was a runaway, and Jesus is the obedient Son.

Daniel saw 'One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven' and receiving an everlasting dominion, Daniel 7:13 and 14. In Matthew 8:20 the title is first used for one who has nowhere to lay His head. That sets the pattern for the Gospel: humiliation first, glory after, Matthew 24:30 and 26:64. The fulfilment is in the one person who is both the homeless Galilean and the ruler of all nations. The correspondence is not yet complete, since the dominion is yet to be displayed, but the title already carries the claim.

typology.type: The conqueror of the demonic powers
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament has little to say about demonic possession, but it knows that evil powers stand behind human enmity and that the LORD will judge them. In the Gospels the kingdom has come, as Jesus says in Matthew 12:28, and the strong man is tied up. Each exorcism is a skirmish in a war that the cross will win, for there, Paul says, Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities,' Colossians 2:15, and Hebrews says He destroyed the one who holds the power of death, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. The demons' words, 'before the appointed time,' show that they know this is a first stage. The type falls short in that the final judgment, Revelation 20:10, is still to come.

The sailors of Psalm 107 cried out in their trouble and the LORD calmed the storm and brought them to their harbour, Psalm 107:28 to 30. The disciples' cry, 'Lord, save us!' is a prayer of the same kind, and in Jesus it receives the same answer. The church has often seen in the boat a picture of its own life, and the New Testament encourages the thought in principle, as it promises that God is with His people in the waters, Isaiah 43:2. The reading must not be pressed into allegory: Matthew does not say that the boat is the church. What he does show is that the presence of Jesus is the safety of those who follow Him.

study.christ:
The three scenes unveil Jesus in three ways, each of which is set against His apparent weakness. In the first, He is the Son of Man who has nowhere to lay His head. That is the human face of the Servant, poorer than the foxes, and yet it is the same speaker who tells the second man that no tie may come before following Him. The poverty and the claim go together. He is not asking others to give what He has not given.

In the second, He sleeps in a boat in a storm. The sleep is a real human tiredness, and the faith that rests in the Father's care: the psalmist could say, 'I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me,' Psalm 3:5. Yet when He wakes, He stills what the psalmist says only the LORD can still, Psalm 89:9. The one who sleeps from weariness and the one who commands the sea are the same, and the disciples' question, 'What kind of man is this?' has only one adequate answer. Their later confession, 'Truly You are the Son of God,' Matthew 14:33, takes it up.

In the third, He is the Son of God before whom the demons shudder. The demons recognise Him as the Son of God and as their judge, 'before the appointed time.' They see the truth that men in the town will not see. The truth is that His coming into their world is already the beginning of the end for them. When He speaks a single word, 'Go!' the whole power of the legion has to obey. Jesus has bound the strong man, Matthew 12:29.

Across these scenes He is also the Lord whose demand is total. He says that the call to follow takes precedence over home and family, Matthew 10:37, and that it involves the cross, Matthew 16:24. A teacher who demands this much must be able to justify it, and He does: the wind and the sea obey Him, and the demons yield. He is trustworthy because He is Lord. The cost is great and the one who asks is greater.

A caution keeps the reading sound. The boat is not an allegory with a coded meaning for every detail, and the pigs are not a picture of something else. The passage does not ask us to look for hidden figures. It asks us to see in each scene the person who does it, and to let the question of verse 27 stand until it is answered.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the Lord of the sea, in a tradition that goes back to the exodus and the psalms. 'You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them,' Psalm 89:9. The Old Testament never suggests that this is a minor attribute. The chaos that threatens creation is under His hand, and Job hears that God has set its boundaries, 'You may come this far, but no farther,' Job 38:11. The disciples' fear tells us that the storm was real, and the calm tells us that it was always under authority. God's people are never in the hands of forces that He does not govern.

The passage shows God as the one whose presence is a refuge in the middle of fear. The question, 'why are you so afraid?' is not a reproach for feeling terror but an invitation to remember who is in the boat. The sleeping Jesus models the trust that rests in the Father, and the waking Jesus shows the power that justifies that trust. Psalm 46:2 and 3 says, 'we will not fear, though the earth is transformed... though their waters roar and foam.' The ground of that confidence is not the absence of storms but the presence of God.

The passage shows God as the Judge of spiritual powers. The demons do not question that there is a time of reckoning, and they dread it. Evil is not an equal rival of God. It is a rebel under sentence, allowed to act within limits, and everything it does is permitted only as far as He allows. The permission is brief and exact, one word, 'Go!' This keeps both the seriousness of evil and the sovereignty of God before us.

The passage shows a God who is kind and who is not safe. The same power that frees two tormented men unsettles a town, and some who see it would rather He left. The God who comes near forces every person to decide, and He leaves them free to say no. This is both a warning and a mercy, for the man who was freed was not forced to go along with a crowd that preferred its pigs.

For worship, the passage invites two things: the honest cry of the boat, 'Lord, save us!' and the awed response of those who see what He has done, 'What kind of man is this?' Both are answered in the God who comes in the person of His Son.

crossReferences.note: Sailors caught in a tempest cry to the LORD, who 'calmed the storm to a whisper,' and brings them to harbour. It is the closest Old Testament pattern for Matthew 8:23 to 27, and it shows why the disciples' reaction is so great: Jesus does what the psalm says the LORD does.

'You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them.' The line comes in a hymn praising the LORD's incomparable power, 'who is like You?' The disciples' question in Matthew 8:27 is the New Testament's echo of that cry.

God asks Job who shut the sea behind doors and told it, 'You may come this far, but no farther.' The authority that Job could not claim is the authority that Jesus exercises when He rebukes the winds and the sea and the waters obey.

Jonah sleeps in a ship in a violent storm and is woken by a captain who asks him to call on his God. The echo is deliberate and the contrast sharp: Jonah's sleep was flight from the LORD, and the storm was his doing, while Jesus' sleep is trust, and the storm calms at His word.

The vision of One like the Son of Man receiving 'dominion, glory, and kingship' over every nation. It is the source of Jesus' favourite self-title, which first appears in Matthew 8:20 in a saying about homelessness and which is the title under which He later claims the final judgment.

Luke gives the same sayings about foxes and the burial of a father, adding a third man who wants to say goodbye to his family. The pattern of three excuses makes clear that Jesus is dealing with a general reluctance, and the line about putting a hand to the plough shows the same urgency.

Elijah lets Elisha kiss his parents goodbye before following. Set beside Matthew 8:21 and 22, it shows the greater urgency of the call of Jesus, who is greater than Elijah, and for whom no farewell may delay the following.

Mark's account of the storm adds that Jesus was in the stern asleep on a cushion, that the disciples asked whether He cared that they were perishing, and that He spoke to the sea, 'Silence! Be still!' Reading it with Matthew 8 shows the same event from two angles, each leaving the disciples with the same question.

Mark gives the longer story of the demoniac in the same region, with the name Legion, the man's request to go with Jesus, and his mission to the Decapolis. It supplies what Matthew leaves out, the sequel in which the one who was freed became a witness, and it contrasts with the town that sent Jesus away.

'Even the demons believe that, and shudder.' The demons in Matthew 8:29 show exactly what James means: they have right belief about Jesus, and it saves no one. Correct confession is not the same as trust, and the town shows that the sight of a miracle is not either.

Paul says Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and triumphed over them by the cross. The authority Jesus uses over the demons in Matthew 8 is a first sign of the victory that the cross wins in full.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God ruling over the deep. In Genesis 1:2 darkness covers the face of the waters, and God's word sets boundaries to the chaos and brings order out of it. The rest of the story keeps returning to the sea as the place where chaos threatens and where God's power is shown, in the flood, the Red Sea, the Jordan and the storms of the psalms. When Jesus gets up in the boat and rebukes the wind, the story of creation is replayed in Galilee: the same word that ordered the deep now rules it again, and the disciples ask the question that the whole Old Testament was meant to raise.

The passage also shows the way into the story's central conflict. Eden was lost to a voice that deceived, Genesis 3:1, and a world under that voice is haunted by powers that destroy human beings, as the two men among the tombs show. In Jesus the kingdom enters their territory. The demons know their time is limited, and the King is not troubled by their threats. The conflict of Genesis 3:15, in which the offspring of the woman is to crush the serpent, is under way. Its decisive battle will be the cross, where Christ 'disarmed the powers,' Colossians 2:15, and its final victory is the day the devil is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

The call to follow takes up the story of Abraham, who left his country and family at God's word, Genesis 12:1, and of Elisha, who followed Elijah. Each had to leave something. The one who calls now is greater than Abraham and Elijah, and His call cuts deeper, because what He gives in return is Himself.

The end of the story answers the storm. In the new creation 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1, not because water is evil but because the threat that the sea stood for is gone, and the one who was asleep in the boat dwells with His people. Until then the disciples sail on, as they did that night, with the Lord in the boat, and with the promise that nothing in all creation, 'neither height nor depth,' will separate them from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:38 and 39.

quiz.q: What did Jesus tell the scribe who offered to follow Him anywhere?

options.text: That the Son of Man has no place to lay His head, naming the cost of following.
options.note: Verse 20 confronts the eager scribe with the homelessness of discipleship.

options.text: That he must first sell all his possessions.
options.note: Jesus stresses homelessness and cost here; the command to sell all is given to another man elsewhere.

options.text: That he was already too sinful to follow.
options.note: Jesus does not reject him as too sinful; He names the cost of following.

options.text: That following Him would bring immediate wealth and comfort.
options.note: The opposite; He warns of having nowhere to lay one's head.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond to the storm on the sea?

options.text: He rebuked the winds and the sea, and it became perfectly calm.
options.note: Verse 26 shows Jesus commanding the storm into stillness by His word.

options.text: He steered the boat safely to shore through the waves.
options.note: He did not merely navigate; He rebuked the elements and they instantly obeyed.

options.text: He prayed and asked God to calm the storm.
options.note: He did not petition; He Himself rebuked the wind and sea with authority.

options.text: He let the storm run its course while reassuring the disciples.
options.note: He actively stilled the storm; He did not merely wait it out.

quiz.q: What question did the disciples ask after the storm was calmed?

options.text: What kind of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?
options.note: Verse 27 records their awe at His authority over nature.

options.text: Why did He wait so long to help them?
options.note: They marveled at who He must be, not primarily at His timing.

options.text: Whether they should find a safer boat.
options.note: Their response was wonder at Jesus' identity, not concern about the boat.

options.text: How He had learned to predict the weather.
options.note: They marveled that the elements obeyed Him, not at any weather knowledge.

quiz.q: What did the demons recognize about Jesus?

options.text: That He is the Son of God and their judge, come at last to torment them at the appointed time.
options.note: Verse 29 has the demons confessing His identity and dreading judgment.

options.text: That He was a powerful exorcist they could resist.
options.note: They knew He was far more, the Son of God, and they could not resist Him at all.

options.text: That He was merely a prophet from Galilee.
options.note: They confess Him Son of God, not merely a prophet.

options.text: That He had no power over them.
options.note: They begged Him, knowing He had complete power to drive them out.

quiz.q: How did the town respond to the deliverance of the demoniacs?

options.text: They were afraid and begged Jesus to leave their region.
options.note: Verse 34 records the town asking Jesus to depart.

options.text: They mourned the loss of their pigs but thanked Jesus.
options.note: They were troubled by the loss, but their actual response was to beg Him to leave, not to thank Him.

options.text: They welcomed Jesus and asked Him to stay and teach.
options.note: The opposite; they asked Him to leave.

options.text: They tried to make Jesus their king.
options.note: Far from crowning Him, they wanted Him gone.

questions: Jesus told the eager scribe about the cost before welcoming his enthusiasm. What has following Jesus cost you, and where are you tempted to want the benefits without the cost?
Jesus said following Him must come before even burying a father. Is there a loyalty, even a good one, that you are allowing to take priority over obeying Christ?
The disciples were rebuked for fear and little faith in the storm. What storm are you facing, and what would it look like to trust that the Lord of wind and wave is in your boat?
The demons recognized Jesus as the Son of God while the townspeople sent Him away. How do you respond when Jesus disturbs your comfort or costs you something you value?
The same Jesus who rules the storm and the demons calls you to follow Him. How does His total authority make His costly call feel not threatening but safe?

translationNotes.note: Son of Man is Jesus' characteristic self-designation, drawn from Daniel 7:13-14, uniting lowliness now with future dominion.
The region is given as the Gadarenes; some manuscripts read Gergesenes or Gerasenes, all naming Gentile territory east of the Sea of Galilee.
Before the appointed time refers to the day of final judgment; the demons know Jesus is their judge and dread their sentence.
